bundles.title: Maryland House of Delegates District 39, 2026 Democratic primary
bundles.coverage_note: Five candidates' full published answers to five common questions, republished from Vote411 by Maryland Matters. The publisher explicitly distinguishes these unedited candidate answers from its edited campaign biographies. Exact pre-primary release/version is unverified, so all answers are downloadable but not enrolled in the dated model corpus. Amar Mukunda is absent from this guide; absence is not a verified nonresponse, withdrawal or no-platform finding.

questions.prompt: Data centers can bring some important economic benefits, but also have a negative impact on the power grid, water supply and land use. Do you support the establishment of additional centers in Maryland? Why or why not?
What do you see as the factors contributing to escalating utility costs in Maryland? How will you address them?
Should the availability of public transportation be improved across the state? Why or why not?
Maryland is required to balance the budget every year. What will be your three top budget priorities, and what programs will you fight for?
Immigrants are an important part of our community and make significant contributions, including to Maryland's economy. What will you do to support immigrant communities in Maryland?

bundles.title: Wisconsin governor, 2026 Democratic primary: housing
bundles.coverage_note: All six tracked Democrats' complete published housing-response blocks from PBS Wisconsin's April22 episode. Named speaker headings delimit answers; reporter narration, the Republican response and Missy Hughes, who is outside this tracked ballot field, are excluded. The transcript preserves edited published responses, not an unedited interview. Source dates do not imply that Barnes or Rodriguez remained active at the August primary.

questions.prompt: A 2024 study by the Wisconsin Policy Forum showed over a five-year stretch, home prices went up 53% while incomes rose by less than 20%. State government can’t lower the price of materials or labor, but it can create an environment making it easier to build new homes. So we asked the candidates for governor how they plan to address the affordable housing crisis in Wisconsin.

bundles.title: Wisconsin governor, 2026 Democratic primary: data centers
bundles.coverage_note: All six tracked Democrats' named response blocks from the February18 PBS episode. Reporter claims in the common introductory prompt are retained as the prompt, not adopted as independently verified facts or included in candidate model text. Hong's response here is not silently expanded into a full moratorium pledge. Candidates may have made additional or later proposals elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Wisconsin’s utility companies are asking the Public Service Commission to approve the largest rate hikes in history. And that’s before we see any impact from the data centers being proposed around the state. So we asked the candidates what role the state should play in approving or facilitating these data centers.

bundles.title: Wisconsin governor, 2026 Democratic primary: school funding and vouchers
bundles.coverage_note: The January30 PBS transcript has two separate named-speaker rounds. Every tracked Democrat's complete published block is preserved for each round. Headings and exact answer ranges prevent another candidate or reporter entering the response. A call for scrutiny is not automatically an abolition pledge, and a candidate's description of current voucher law is not independently certified legal guidance.

questions.prompt: Calling Wisconsin’s school funding formula broken is one of the oldest refrains in state politics, but the sheer number and size of operating referenda around the state show school districts and voters agree the state is not providing enough money.

Wisconsin’s school voucher program was created in the 1990s in Milwaukee and expanded statewide in 2011. As the cost of the program has grown, the question we put to the candidates is whether it should expand, contract or stay the same.

bundles.title: Wisconsin governor, 2026 Democratic primary: first governing priorities
bundles.coverage_note: All six tracked candidates' answers to PBS's first-bill prompt, published January16. The interview dates precede later withdrawals. These explicitly stated priorities support campaign-framing comparisons, not measured message frequency or proof that unmentioned policies were opposed. The publisher's Francesa Hong name typo is explicitly reviewed and retained in the source heading.

questions.prompt: For the first time in 16 years, you can legitimately say control of the Wisconsin Legislature is up for grabs in the next election, which means the incoming governor could actually pass their agenda. So we asked each candidate what the first bill would be that they want to sign into law. The most common answer had to do with dealing with the rising costs of everything.

bundles.title: Wisconsin governor, 2026 Democratic primary: cross-party governing
bundles.coverage_note: Six complete named responses from the January21 PBS episode. Claimed legislative accomplishments remain attributed self-descriptions. The publisher's Joe Brennan heading is explicitly associated with the canonical Joel Brennan record through the same original interview series. These answers do not justify assuming the DSA-endorsed candidate rejects all bipartisan work.

questions.prompt: With a Democratic governor and a Republican Legislature, the last eight years in Wisconsin politics have been defined by gridlock and a lack of trust in the Capitol. And whether a Democrat or Republican wins the race for governor this fall, there’s a good chance the other party will control at least one chamber of the Legislature, meaning the next governor will need to know how to work across the aisle to pass a budget. We asked nine of the leading candidates for governor about their track record of bipartisanship.

bundles.title: Hawaii Congressional District 1, 2018 Democratic primary

bundles.title: Pittsburgh City Council District 7, 2023 Democratic primary
bundles.coverage_note: Both candidates answered WESA's five questions. Candidate answers are separated from reporter biographies and source captions. Numerical claims about housing output, buyers and budgets remain attributed statements rather than independently verified statistics.

questions.prompt: What should Pittsburgh City Council’s top priority be right now? How would you try to address it, if elected?
What does your district most need from City Council? Why are you the right person to address it?
Violent crime, particularly among youth, has been a high priority for the mayor’s office and city council. What do you think council’s role should be in addressing the problem?
variants: Violent crime, particularly among youth, has been an issue of high priority for the mayor’s office and city council. What do you think council’s role should be in addressing the problem?

questions.prompt: Pittsburgh faces a variety of housing challenges — from a lack of affordable housing stock to a growing homeless population. What is the most effective thing council can do to address this?
variants: Pittsburgh faces a variety of housing challenges — from a lack of affordable housing stock to a growing homeless population — what is the most effective thing council can do to address this?

questions.prompt: The state of the city’s Bureau of Police has been a topic of discussion for city leaders. While City Council has held public hearings to learn more about staffing concerns, what else can or should council do to improve working conditions for police?

bundles.title: Allegheny County Council District 11, 2023 Democratic primary
bundles.coverage_note: Both candidates answered all five WESA questions. Complete responses retain shared opposition to privatizing Shuman, support for more council resources, and differing policy emphases without treating an unmentioned proposal as opposed.

questions.prompt: What is the most important issue for residents of your district? What will you do to tackle that issue?

Allegheny County’s property tax assessment system has been subject to much criticism in recent months. How do you think property tax assessments should be handled going forward, and what steps will you take to accomplish that?

County Council has passed a number of environmental ordinances during the past year, including a ban on fracking in county parks and creating a new Department of Sustainability. But there is still debate on issues such as the county's approach to large industrial polluters. What changes, if any, would you like to see in the county's energy and environmental policies, and why?

Conditions at the Allegheny County Jail have become a subject of intense debate, and there is increased discussion of finding a replacement for the now-closed Shuman Juvenile Detention Center. What concerns, if any, do you have about the future for these facilities, and what would you do on council to address those concerns?

County Council has played a more activist role in recent years, sometimes thwarting the county executive's agenda and pursuing its own policy goals. Critics say council is a part-time body whose role was originally intended to simply oversee the county's budget process. What role do you think council should play in shaping policy, and do you think council needs more staff and resources than it has now?

bundles.title: Allegheny County Controller, 2023 Democratic primary
bundles.coverage_note: Both candidates answered WESA's five questions before the primary. Accusations, self-described records and financial assessments remain attributed statements, not independent audit findings. The candidate answers are separated from reporter biographies and captions.

questions.prompt: The controller's office has oversight over county operations and agencies. What areas of government require the most urgent scrutiny, and why?
How would you assess the availability and transparency of information about the county's finances and operations, and what, if anything, do you think should the next controller do to improve it?

A controller acts as a fiscal watchdog, and an ability to maintain independence from the legislative and executive branch of the government is arguably essential. What can you point to in your background to demonstrate that independence?

The controller sits on the Jail Oversight Board, as well as a juvenile detention advisory board, and a retirement and investment board. How well are these boards functioning in your view, and what role do you think you would play on them as controller?
How would you assess the county's overall financial strength, and what fiscal concerns would you be paying attention to as controller?

bundles.title: Fairfax County Braddock District, 2019 Democratic primary
bundles.coverage_note: Both candidates' complete responses to GGWash's six housing and transportation questions are retained. Explicit speaker prefixes and paragraph ranges separate the interleaved answers. Stated fiscal amounts, population statistics and claimed effects are candidate assertions, not independent audit findings.

questions.prompt: Who do you think has the hardest time finding housing that’s affordable to them in Fairfax County, and what steps do you plan to take to address that need?
Would you champion increasing housing diversity in parts of the county which have fewer lower-income residents than the entire county and Washington region as a whole? Why or why not?
How do you reconcile the need to provide housing affordability in the parts of your district with good transit with some other people’s stated desire to slow development?

Fairfax County has been pushing for walkable, transit-accessible communities to meet demand and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from transportation. Would you continue this trend, and where in your district would you emphasize this? If not, why not?
What are the top three transportation priorities you have for your district? Tell us why and the revenue source (including any new revenue sources you’d champion).

Fairfax County is one of the few area jurisdictions that has not adopted Vision Zero. Given the high number of people who die or are seriously injured while moving around in Fairfax, what would you advocate to ensure safety for everyone even though Fairfax DOT has to work with VDOT to make changes in Fairfax’s transportation network?
